title: Nepal requests $20 million from loss and damage fund after floods — Deutsche Welle - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal requests $20 million from loss and damage fund after floods — Deutsche Welle  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal has requested $20 million from the UN-backed international Loss and Damage Fund after August floods and landslides that killed more than 1,400 people, while thousands are considered missing. Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary said this in an interview with Deutsche Welle English.

According to Chaudhary, the government has already sent an official letter to the fund, and most states have responded positively. The flash floods caused extensive damage to housing, agricultural land and infrastructure. Rescue and recovery operations are still underway in several areas, while authorities assess the overall scale of the damage.

Demand for climate justice

The minister said Nepal needs not only words of sympathy, but also justice. She called on countries with the highest emissions and financial capabilities to pay for the consequences of climate disasters suffered by vulnerable states.

Nepal accounts for approximately 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, but its mountainous geography makes the country particularly vulnerable to climate risks. Rising temperatures in the Himalayas are accelerating glacier retreat and increasing the risks of glacial lake outburst floods, landslides and extreme weather events.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Chaudhary linked the latest disaster to climate change, citing glacier melt, warming and changes in the mountain environment. At the same time, the article notes that detailed attribution studies are usually needed to establish a causal link between a specific disaster and global warming. Researchers may take into account a combination of factors, including glacier and permafrost degradation, extreme weather and geological vulnerability.

Plans ahead of COP31

Nepal intends to seek greater recognition of the specific challenges facing mountain countries at the COP31 climate conference, scheduled for November in Turkey. According to the minister, Kathmandu will also raise the consequences of the floods and the need for concrete international support at the UN General Assembly.

Following the disaster, the government is also reviewing its early warning systems. Chaudhary acknowledged that the existing mechanisms did not cope with the scale of the disaster, although residents received messages and information. Nepal is working with China to monitor river systems and glacial threats that cross state borders.

title: Biting the hand that feeds: Nepal demands climate cash while blaming us for its disaster - Washington Examiner
description: Biting the hand that feeds: Nepal demands climate cash while blaming us for its disaster  Washington Examiner
publisher.title: Washington Examiner
full_article:
Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal’s request for a foreign response to his country’s disastrous Himalayan flood would be better made as an appeal to the charitable instincts of people than as a demand for compensation from climate sinners.

Khanal connects the Aug. 26 flood to the popular narrative that industrial emissions of carbon dioxide cause dangerous atmospheric warming and the melting of mountain glaciers, which, so the logic goes, produces floods like the one that killed his countrymen. “Climate justice” reasoning is that industrialized countries such as neighboring India and China bear more responsibility for the disaster than Nepal, whose per capita income ranking is less than five on a global scale of 1-100.

Recommended Stories Trump is fighting Canada on trade — so why are we letting it rob our waters? Stop treating election night like the season finale — it’s really the series premiere Trump can’t stand what football does to America

Khanal’s framing begins with a vacuous political claim that someone else must pay and ignores realities of the physical world, adopting the false premise that CO2 emissions have made the weather worse. He apparently embraces the notion that computer models can assign a dollar value to damages inflicted by increases in the destructiveness of natural disasters. For the foreign minister, an apocalyptic narrative used for a decade to advance net-zero policy is an observed fact rather than an implausibly extreme scenario treated as destiny.

Advertisement

A century of observations shows no CO2-driven march toward more heat waves, hurricanes, droughts, and wildfires. Many of those hazards peaked in earlier decades or have declined. Record U.S. heat still belongs to the 1930s. Hurricane activity has not followed the alarmist script. Wildfire intensity is inseparable from fuel loads and land management. A report by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine that “quantifies climate damages” merely assumes worsening weather with rising CO2 without even attempting to establish a link. The National Academies uses computer-generated models of a world with no industrial CO2 emissions to divine how much milder the weather would be. That is a fabrication for use in a liability case, not a finding of fact. Studies that purportedly attribute worsening weather to emissions have multiplied because “climate scientists” have been rewarded with research grants, not because physics demonstrates evidence of a connection. Saying the Nepal flood would have been milder on a planet without industrial CO2 is not evidence that floods have grown more common or more destructive. Advertisement Once those exercises are treated as proof of causation, Nepal’s Khanal would say, energy producers “whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours” are to be made defendants in civil courts facing billions of dollars in liabilities. This demagoguery makes villains of businesses whose products — coal, oil, and natural gas — have powered electric grids, transportation systems, and factories that have lifted living standards worldwide. The fertilizers and medicines derived from these hydrocarbon feedstocks nourish and enhance the health of billions. Nepal’s own development depends on fossil fuels. Transport runs on imported diesel and gasoline. Cooking and industry use liquefied petroleum gas and coal. Coal is necessary for cement production, which is integral to the infrastructure of the country’s hydroelectric system and highways. Asian neighbors and Western countries demonized for “climate failings” have supported Nepal’s building of high-voltage lines, tunnels, bridges, vehicles, and other blessings of modernity. Foreign Minister Khanal is biting the hands engaged in feeding his country. Advertisement None of this diminishes the tragedy of the thousands of dead and missing in August’s awful flood. Nonetheless, compassion does not require surrendering facts to accommodate what amounts to a scam. There is no evidence of carbon dioxide emissions precipitating the Nepal flood or any other disaster. Even the U.N. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has declared its most extreme predictions of global warming implausible. The most likely cause of the flood has been identified as the failure of bedrock underlying a glacier. HOW RADICAL ENVIRONMENTALISTS TURNED YOUR RETIREMENT ACCOUNT INTO CLIMATE COLLATERAL More than climate apostates to blame, Nepal needs modern technology and better land-use practices to protect people as much as possible from the risk of nature’s brutality. Advertisement In the meantime, the country has reportedly received $820 million in aid, which suggests that at least some in the developed world are more charitable than villainous. Angela Wheeler is executive director of the CO2 Coalition in Fairfax, Virginia. She is a cum laude graduate of Emporia State University, Kansas, where she studied communication, with additional biology and pre-medicine coursework.

title: Hindutva Is Slowly Seeping Into Nepal - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
description: Hindutva Is Slowly Seeping Into Nepal  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
publisher.title: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
full_article:
On the night of July 26 , a Hindu procession was on its way back after collecting holy water from the Koshi River. The procession being taken out at Kaptanganj of Sunsari district in eastern Nepal was accompanied by loud music, to which some local Muslims objected. A scuffle broke out. Police got involved.

Hindu-Muslim tensions soon spread across Nepal’s Tarai-Madhesh belt, the east-west strip of land abutting India. In ensuing clashes between protesters and the police, four people died while curfews disrupted life across the region.

Such incidents follow a recognizable pattern. One newspaper investigation identified 17 Hindu-Muslim documented clashes over the past decade – with around two-thirds of them involving religious processions or idol immersions. The number of undocumented cases is undoubtedly higher.

The History

Over the past decade or so the influx of Hindutva ideas from India has been steadily stoking Hindu-Muslim tensions. Before that, these communities had mostly lived in harmony in a country where over 80 percent of people are Hindus. Muslims, by contrast, make up just 5 percent of the national population. But seldom did this small religious minority feel persecuted. After the recent devastating floods , the coming together of people from different faiths to help and pray for victims offered a glimpse of the inter-faith harmony Nepal has long been known for.

For most of its modern history, Nepal has been a de facto Hindu state. Prithvi Narayan Shah, the 18th-century founder of modern Nepal, famously described his kingdom as Asal Hindustan , or the “real Hindustan.” He wanted to build “a true home for Hindus” at a time when much of the Indian subcontinent was under Muslim rule.

The 1962 constitution promulgated by King Mahendra was the first to officially declare Nepal as a Hindu kingdom, with the divine monarch as its protector. After this, the 1990 charter introduced following a popular movement heralded a constitutional monarchy but kept the Hindu state characterization.

Things would drastically change in 2006 following the end of the decade-long Maoist insurgency and the second people’s movement. The interim constitution promulgated a year later held in abeyance the institution of the monarchy – which was later abolished by the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly – and formally declared Nepal a secular state.

Yet with the Maoists losing electoral ground in the second Constituent Assembly election in 2013, conservative forces began to reassert themselves. This is why the new (and currently operative) constitution promulgated in 2015 gave continuity to Nepal’s secular designation but added a rider: Nepali secularism would entail the “protection of religion and culture being practiced since ancient times.”

As the new charter was being finalized, the country’s secularism debate was also being closely watched in India. Hindu nationalist politicians and organizations there were openly lobbying for the restoration of Nepal’s Hindu status.

Narendra Modi’s election as Indian prime minister in 2014 had given the cause an added impetus. But the new Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) establishment in New Delhi wouldn’t get its way.

It was partly because Nepal’s secular status was retained in the 2015 charter that India imposed a crippling, four-and-a-half-month-long blockade on the land-locked country.

As Nepal was struggling to finalize its constitution and consolidate its status as a secular republic, Hindu nationalist politics was becoming dominant across its southern border. Hindutva ideas, symbols, and organizations started making greater inroads into Nepal.

For and Against a Hindu State

Hindutva is a right-wing ideology that seeks to organize all Hindus as a political community. It portrays Hindu civilization as coming under threat from other religions like Islam and Christianity whose origins lie outside India.

There are compelling arguments for why a wholesale import of Hindutva is unlikely in Nepal.

Richard Bownas, a scholar who has been closely following Hindu politics in Nepal, argued that the kind of “ actionable package ” that makes mass Hindu mobilization for political ends so effective in India is absent in Nepal. For instance, Nepal has only around 250 active shakhas of the Hindu Swayamsevak Sangh (HSS), an offshoot of the Rastriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist volunteer paramilitary organization closely associated with the BJP.

The HSS has made rapid inroads into Nepal. Still, the country has just one shakha for every 120,000 people, in comparison to one for 17,000 people in India. Nepal’s heterogeneous religious landscape as well as the lack of religious zealotry of its political leadership, Bownas argued, also prevent Hindutva from exerting the same kind of influence.

But with ideological politics taking a backseat and populists now running Nepal, there is a distinct possibility of a greater embrace of religion as a political tool by ruling and opposition parties alike. Early signs are that the government of Balendra Shah formed after the 2025 Gen Z uprising and March 2026 elections is partial to Hinduism.

The new prime minister’s inauguration ceremony was steeped in Hindu Vedic rituals, making people of other faiths suspect the credentials of the head of government of a secular state. Even the recent ceremony to mark the first anniversary of the Gen Z protests drew controversy over the presence of certain Hindu religious leaders.

The ruling ideology-lite Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), it appears, will find the allure of Hinduism as a political weapon hard to resist.

The top leaders of more established political parties, which were trounced in the March 2026 general elections, also see religion as perhaps the only tool that can pave the way for their unlikely comeback.

Sher Bahadur Deuba , five-time prime minister and long-time leader of the Nepali Congress, traditionally the country’s biggest democratic force, has of late been openly flaunting his Hindu identity and emphasizing the country’s Hindu roots. Until now the committed secularist had been resisting the call of a vocal Congress faction to lobby for the restoration of the Hindu state.

K.P. Sharma Oli, the three-time prime minister and current chair of the Communist Party of Nepal-Unified Marxist-Leninist (CPN-UML), the country’s biggest communist outfit, has been courting Nepali Hindus for much longer. Among his infamous anti-India post-blockade pitches was the claim that Ram, a central deity in Hindutva mobilization, was born in Thori of Nepal rather than across the border in Ayodhya of India.

It is becoming clear that as older ideological distinctions like social democracy, communism, monarchy, and regionalism lose their mobilization power, religion is increasingly likely to fill the vacuum.

Two trends make the present moment different: the weakening of Nepal’s older political identities and the ready availability of a Hindu nationalist vocabulary from across the border.

In order to reshape Nepali politics, Hindutva does not have to look exactly the same as it does in India. Local politicians can borrow its symbols, grievances, and methods of mobilization and adapt them to their political circumstances.

That process is especially salient in the Tarai-Madhesh belt.

Saffronization of the Plains

For decades, political mobilization in Nepal’s plains – which constitutes less than 25 percent of the country’s landmass but is home to over 50 percent of its people – revolved around caste, regional exclusion, identity, and demands for representation within the Nepali state. This was especially true of Madhesh Province, the epicenter of Madheshi identity politics.

With the RSP sweeping the last general elections – winning 30 of 32 seats in the province – traditional Madheshi parties have been greatly weakened.

The erosion of ideological and regional loyalties, as has been seen in Madhesh, has prompted local politicians to try to regain their influence by presenting themselves as defenders of the “Hindu community” or “Muslim community.” This was also evident in the aftermath of the Kaptanganj clashes.

More broadly, the rise of the BJP in India, culminating symbolically in the inauguration of the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya in 2024, has coincided with more conspicuous and competitive displays of religious identity in Nepal.

Saffron pennants are increasingly visible on Hindu homes and neighborhoods in the Tarai-Madhesh – thanks in part to sustained activism of the HSS foot soldiers who encourage such displays of Hindu religiosity. Green religious flags are similarly displayed by Muslims. Religious processions are often larger, louder, and more assertive.

Before the July 26 incident, the local Hindu community in Kaptanganj was apparently unhappy because some of the green pennants planted during the Muslim festival of Muharram a month before were not uprooted at the festival’s end. Once a procession or flag is interpreted as demonstrating which community controls a road, neighborhood, or public space, minor disputes can take on existential significance.

The Tarai-Madhesh is vulnerable to the allure of Hindutva also because of geography. Nepal and India share an open border and the neighboring Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh are the heartlands of Hindu nationalist politics. Communities on the two sides have “roti-beti relations” as they are tied together by marriage, trade, pilgrimage, language, and culture.

Political ideas thus cross the border as easily as people do. This also makes it easy for organizations like the RSS – whose ideology Indian historian Ram Chandra Guha distilled as “We will show Muslims their place” – to operate in the belt.

The Corrosive Effects of Social Media

Social media has dramatically accelerated religious polarization.

Many participants in the Kaptanganj protests had hurried to the incident site after seeing provocative videos and messages on their mobile phones. Instant social media amplification then spread the clashes across the Tarai-Madhesh belt.

In the past, an argument over a flag or procession in one Tarai village would remain confined there. Local party representatives, elders, and community leaders would intervene before an argument acquired a wider communal character. Increasingly, the mediators themselves arrive as representatives of religious constituencies.

This in turn can contribute to polarization along religious lines. Once members of a religion feel politically or physically insecure, they have an incentive to mobilize on the basis of their religion.

Today, audio and video footage of a communal clash can spread across Nepal and among the diaspora communities around the world within minutes.

Videos are often stripped of context and accompanied by inflammatory claims. Hindu and Muslim influencers circulate clips portraying their respective communities as victims. Old footage can be rehashed as evidence of new attacks.

Social media changes the geographical scale of communal tensions. A local dispute between neighbors becomes an event in a much larger Hindu-Muslim struggle. That makes traditional local mediation much more difficult.

Radicalization and Demographic Fear

The emerging Hindu nationalist narrative in the Tarai-Madhesh is anti-Muslim. Yet the larger national narrative is of Hindu demographic and cultural vulnerability.

Christianity is another focus of Hindu mobilization (although this is more of an issue up in the hilly regions than down in the Tarai plains). Royalist and Hindu nationalist groups frequently claim that aggressive Christian proselytization, backed by foreign money, is eroding Nepal’s traditional culture. Opposition to conversion has consequently become intertwined with campaigns to restore Hindu statehood.

Supporters of Hindu political mobilization argue that secularism was surreptitiously introduced during Nepal’s turbulent political transition without a popular mandate. They point to Christian conversion, greater activity of foreign-funded religious organizations, and “ Islamist radicalization ” as the unwanted consequences. Restoring Nepal’s Hindu identity, they believe , would protect rather than divide society.

The debate over Nepal’s religious identity predates Modi and the recent communal clashes. Even the constitution reflects that unresolved tension by simultaneously declaring Nepal secular and promising protection for religions and cultures practiced since ancient times.

Hindu nationalist narratives also increasingly portray Nepal’s Hindu majority as endangered. Some YouTubers and news channels have attributed recent communal disturbances to Rohingya Muslim refugees allegedly entering Nepal from Bangladesh.

But the vast majority of Nepal’s Muslims are not a recently arrived population – nor has their presence caused any problem for much of Nepal’s modern history. They are established Nepali communities, overwhelmingly concentrated in the Tarai, often speaking the same languages and participating in the same local economies as their Hindu neighbors.

Some of these concerns deserve factual scrutiny. Religious radicalization and illicit foreign financing should not be ignored wherever credible evidence exists. Nepali laws ban forced conversation; the challenge is their judicious implementation.

State Failure and Elite Apathy

The Nepali state has responded poorly to this emerging challenge.

Even as communal tensions simmered across the Tarai-Madhesh during the latest crisis, Shah, the prime minister, remained silent for several days. He addressed the nation only after the unrest had spread and the situation was threatening to get out of control. Security institutions also appear poorly prepared to handle communal violence.

The problem is not just inadequate riot-control capacity. Resolution of communal conflict calls for local knowledge, trusted intermediaries, early intelligence, and officials capable of distinguishing between a normal religious celebration and an organized attempt at provocation. Nepal’s security forces frequently lack those advantages.

Provinces still do not have the degree of independent policing authority envisioned by the constitution, leaving crucial decisions to officials in Kathmandu. There is also an old perception in the Madhesh that Kathmandu’s political and bureaucratic establishment treats violence in the plains as somehow peripheral to the country’s central political life.

The most troubling aspect is that the violence in Kaptanganj was foreseeable.

The Armed Police Force warned the government years ago that organized actors were fanning religious and ethnic tensions in the Tarai and recommended political and administrative intervention. Yet the state continued to see such tensions principally as a law-and-order problem and failed to prepare for the worst.

Crossing a Threshold?

Is Nepal crossing a dangerous threshold whereby every major political force feels the need to employ Hinduism as a political tool? That would be unfortunate. One of the hallmarks of post-1990 Nepali politics has been the ability of Nepali political parties to come together to face moments of national crisis.

This was most clearly visible in 2015. That year, after the devastating earthquakes had brought the country to a standstill, parties from across the political spectrum set aside their ideological differences to promulgate the new constitution and put national politics back on track.

After Kaptanganj too, the parties eventually came together to call for calm. But compromise will become harder when politics is built around sacred identities. The recent clashes are warning signs of a potentially much larger transformation in Nepali politics.

Nepal is not India. Its history, social structure, and religious traditions are different. The syncretic nature of Nepali society and its long record of coexistence protect against wholesale import of India’s communal politics.

title: In Nepal’s flood, people with disabilities faced barriers, first in rescue and now in recovery - The World from PRX
description: In Nepal’s flood, people with disabilities faced barriers, first in rescue and now in recovery  The World from PRX
publisher.title: The World from PRX
full_article:
When the flood hit Syabrubesi in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, Pratima Lama survived only because of her daughter. Misan, 9, saw the flood rush through the town and hit the market. She grabbed her mother’s hand and pulled her toward the door.

“I just tried to run uphill as far as I could,” said Lama, 40, speaking through an interpreter. “I asked other people for help, but they couldn’t. Everyone was running for their own lives.”

View Image: 2026-09-22-Nepal-disabilities-Lama-and-daughter-1024x768.jpeg Pratima Lama and her daughter, Misan, at a shelter in Kathmandu. Hannah Chanatry/The World

Lama is blind. As they ran, she was entirely dependent on her daughter to get them to safety.

People with disabilities are disproportionately affected by climate change. According to research, people with disabilities are up to four times more likely to die or be injured in a climate-driven disaster like the flood in Nepal. A new analysis from World Weather Attribution determined that climate change destabilized the region, degrading the glacier and likely weakening the bedrock, before the bedrock ultimately collapsed in a rock-ice avalanche.

Those disproportionate impacts extend to the relief and recovery systems that spring up after a disaster; these systems often overlook the specialized needs people may have for healthcare, accommodation or communication.

‘Not very disability friendly‘

“It’s not very disability-friendly,” said Lama about the shelter where she and her daughter now live. About 300 survivors from their town were relocated to a Buddhist monastery in Kathmandu.

“The toilets are far away,” she said, “and after the first two nights I developed a fever.”

Lama was able to reach a cousin living elsewhere in Kathmandu. She and Misan now stay there during the night, and they return to the monastery every day for meals and information about their town. Lama said the people running the shelter are doing a good job, but she couldn’t manage the stairs, the distances or the crowds, especially after she lost her white cane for navigating through the floodwaters.

Accessibility problems are also widespread for survivors who are deaf, according to Bishwamitra Bhitrakoti, a deaf advocate and communications officer with the National Federation of the Deaf Nepal. He traveled to Devighat and Bidur, two other towns with significant flood damage, and found a glaring issue: no sign language interpreters.

View Image: 2026-09-22-Nepal-disabilities-governent-aid-trucks-1024x768.jpeg Betrawati Baazar, one of the towns devastated by the flood. Hannah Chanatry/The World

He said this is a common problem across several shelters.

“Some deaf people, they don’t even know the Nepali sign language,” said Bhitrakoti. They still use “natural sign language” in the remote villages, he said, “so it’s not [formal] sign language, [but] gestures or something to communicate with people.

Dawa Furi Tamang, 63, has struggled at the same monastery shelter as Lama for exactly that reason. He’s mostly deaf and cannot communicate verbally. He was also never taught Nepali sign language.

Because no interpreters were on site, an independent sign language interpreter joined The World at the monastery to speak with Tamang. The conversation required additional interpretation from Tamang’s relative, who was also displaced by the flood. Each knew only some natural sign language, and they worked together to help Tamang describe his experience.

He’s frustrated, said Tamang, that it is so hard to communicate more widely and to get around independently. He’s also afraid he’ll be unable to get a job in Kathmandu or have financial security in the future.

The “government did not support us until now,” he said through both interpreters. He told The World that the organization of relief supplies has been unreliable and that those supplies are not always going where they are needed most.

View Image: 2026-09-22-Nepal-disabilities-Bazaar-1024x768.jpeg Government aid trucks trying to get to the Rasuwa district from Kathmandu. The drive takes several hours along a muddy, narrow mountain pass. Hannah Chanatry/The World

Nepal’s government has specific plans for disability inclusion within its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, as well as within its National Adaptation Plan. However, some advocates The World spoke to have argued that these high-level plans are not successfully implemented at the community level.

The World has not yet received a comment from the Nepali government.

Search and rescue continues

More than 1,400 people are confirmed dead, and more than 6,000 are missing, according to revisions to government data as of Sept. 17th.

It’s been more than 20 days since the disaster; by now, Nepal should have entered what experts call an “early recovery period,” according to Saagar Shrestha, director of the disaster management department at Nepal’s Red Cross Society. That typically involves shifting the focus from immediate, life-saving supplies to longer-term support.

View Image: 2026-09-22-Nepal-floods-building-damage-1024x683.jpg Ruined buildings and blocks of concrete in Betrawati Baazar. Hannah Chanatry/The World

“This is something different,” said Shrestha, adding that his team has still been unable to get that first wave of supplies to parts of the Rasuwa district. The flood destroyed access to the more remote villages, except by helicopter, and those helicopters are in use in the ongoing search and rescue operations.

Once they can begin the more formal recovery process, Shrestha said, the Red Cross will prioritize sending aid to people with disabilities, along with children, pregnant women, and the elderly. His team is still putting together data on how many people with disabilities were affected by the flood — just under 3% of the population in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts had a documented disability, according to the national census, though Shrestha said that is likely an undercount.

“[The] disaster perspective, before this incident and after, absolutely [needs] to change,” he said. We need to “train ourselves differently, even our mindset.”

There is growing momentum to increase disability awareness in Nepal and to take disabilities into greater consideration during emergency planning. For the past several years, the Red Cross has trained its staff and volunteers on how to evacuate people with a range of disabilities during a disaster; it has also trained people with disabilities on how to evacuate themselves until help arrives.

However, ultimately, Shrestha said he’s unsure if Nepal will ever truly be a “disability-friendly country.”

“You see the mountain, the terrain,” he said. “Every kilometer, the climate is different; the landscape is different.” The financial investment across all the differences, he said, would be astronomical.

“Even if you have the perfect early warning system, those people who are living with disabilities, especially living in [that] particular terrain,” may be very difficult to get to, he said.

This was not Nepal’s first deadly flood, said Shrestha, and while the severity of this flood was unprecedented, it will not be the last. Nepal has more than 3,000 glaciers and is warming nearly twice as fast as the global average. Glacial melt and thawing permafrost across the Himalaya are destabilizing the region, causing more landslides and increasing the risk of glacial floods.

full_article:
Binay Shah, President of the Binaytara, shared on LinkedIn:

“I’m pleased to share this article published in The Rising Nepal, where I highlight a crucial healthcare initiative addressing cervical cancer in Madhes Province.

Cervical cancer is almost entirely preventable, yet it remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths among women in Nepal. In this piece, I look at how the global cancer non-profit Binaytara is tackling this in Janakpur by pairing HPV-based screening with trusted Female Community Health Volunteers (FCHVs).

We found women with secondary education were over 4 times more likely to be aware of cervical cancer, while those with decision-making autonomy showed far better understanding of screening benefits.

Binaytara is scaling up to screen 1000+ women while actively involving male volunteers to build household support. Preventable deaths shouldn’t happen due to systemic gaps. It’s time for policymakers to scale these proven community models nationwide.

Thank you Meghan Clarke for your support.

title: Analysis: Nepal’s $20m ‘loss-and-damage’ claim only covers 0.7% of flood costs - Carbon Brief
description: Analysis: Nepal’s $20m ‘loss-and-damage’ claim only covers 0.7% of flood costs  Carbon Brief
publisher.title: Carbon Brief
full_article:
Home Policy International policy Analysis: Nepal’s $20m ‘loss-and-damage’ claim only covers 0.7% of flood costs 22.09.26 International policy By: Aruna Chandrasekhar, Josh Gabbatiss A woman stands near homes damaged by flash floods in Dhunge Bazar, Nuwakot district, Nepal, on 12 September 2026. Credit: Aryan Dhimal / Alamy Stock Photo

Print article Share

Article Contents Expand menu Close Nepal’s needs

Requests vs pledges

‘Rapid response’

The Nepali government has requested $20m from the UN fund for “loss and damage”, following the devastating floods that hit the country in late August.

This amounts to just 0.7% of the $2.7bn it has estimated in “physical damage” to infrastructure and “economic losses” from the flooding, according to Carbon Brief analysis.

The $20m request would, nevertheless, make Nepal the fourth-largest claimant to the UN loss-and-damage fund, which is intended to help deal with climate-related disasters.

Developing countries have already made 176 applications to the UN fund for responding to loss and damage, requesting, in total, $2.8bn to help recover from a variety of damaging events, such as drought, floods and storms.

Yet, to date, predominantly developed nations have only pledged $0.8bn to support the fund.

This means requests to the fund are already three times larger than the total amount pledged, raising questions about its potential to respond to emergencies.

As yet, no funding has been paid out of the fund to developing countries grappling with intensifying and more frequent climate change-induced disasters since it was established in 2023.

Nepal’s needs

On 26 August, Nepal was hit by flash floods following a catastrophic rock-ice avalanche in the Himalayan border region. The flooding has killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing.

Days later, the Nepali government sought an “urgent response” from the board of the UN fund for climate-driven loss and damage.

It subsequently requested $20m in “financial compensation” from the fund. This is the maximum amount that can currently be requested for a single project.

“Loss and damage” is a term used to describe how climate change is causing serious and, in many cases, irreversible impacts around the world. Nations established the UN fund in 2023, after decades of effort by climate-vulnerable nations.

Nepal’s national disaster management authority has now released an extensive rapid preliminary assessment of “damage and needs” from the floods.

As the chart below shows, Nepal’s $20m loss-and-damage claim would only cover 0.7% of what authorities describe as $2.7bn in “total damage and loss” from the floods.

When accounting for another $4.8bn in “recovery and reconstruction” costs – part of how loss and damage is internationally defined – then Nepal’s $20m claim would be just 0.3% of the needs it estimates.



Reacting to the analysis, Nepal’s climate negotiator Raju Pandit Chhetri tells Carbon Brief that the country’s $20m request was for “rapid response”, adding:

“That money is going to be a peanut if it was to be invested into reconstruction.”

Requests vs pledges

Vulnerable, developing countries have long argued that developed nations should be held responsible for loss and damage, while countries such as the US have blocked moves that could have led to them being liable for climate-related damages

From December 2025 until July 2026, developing countries made 176 applications to the loss-and-damage fund, requesting over $2.8bn in assistance.

So far, predominantly developed countries have pledged only $822m to the fund. (Some nations that are not categorised as “developed” under the UN, such as the UAE and South Korea, have also committed funds.)

Funding requests from developing countries to date are, therefore, more than triple what has been pledged.

Apart from Nepal’s new request, “requested” data is based on the project pipeline as of 29 June 2026. Analysis by Carbon Brief.

Moreover, only around half of the money pledged so far has been paid into the fund by donor nations, with large sums from France, Italy and the UAE still outstanding.

The fund has made $342m available in its initial funding round in July 2026. However, as of September, no money from the fund has been distributed to any countries facing climate-related disasters.

According to Carbon Brief analysis, off the 176 loss-and-damage fund requests received from 118 countries, more than 60% are from least developed countries – such as Nepal – and small-island nations. So far, each individual funding request is capped at $20m.

The flood-related request is Nepal’s fourth appeal to the fund and, as the chart below shows, this makes it the fourth-largest claimant overall.

Apart from Nepal’s new request, data is based on the project pipeline as of 29 June 2026. Analysis by Carbon Brief.

Nine other countries have made multiple requests to the fund. Madagascar – hit by back-to-back cyclones after a prolonged drought – has made six requests in total.

Drought-ravaged Suriname, Ecuador, Brazil and Barbados have specified that their funding requests are part of an “emergency response”.

‘Rapid response’

Nepal’s $20m claim has sparked a conversation on climate justice and the ability of the loss-and-damage fund to deliver, in the face of increasingly frequent extreme-weather events.

In a letter sent five days after the disaster, Nepal’s finance minister Dr Swarnim Wagle appealed to the fund’s board to mobilise an “urgent response” that would “signal” that the fund:

“[I]s capable of responding with humanity, speed, flexibility and solidarity when climate-vulnerable countries face losses and damages beyond their capacity to address alone.”

Board members from Asia-Pacific and African countries wrote a letter in support of the Himalayan country in crisis, urging the board to convene and “potentially agree to a provisional set-aside allocation of resources to support rapid response funding for Nepal”.

They pointed out that the board’s response to Nepal could offer “procedural lessons” in how to strengthen its “rapid-response” to sudden-onset extreme-weather events. Such support is explicitly part of the fund’s mandate.

On 14 September, developed-country members of the fund’s board wrote that they supported a “consultation” on Nepal, but made no commitments in terms of actual funding.

Harjeet Singh, loss-and-damage expert and global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, tells Carbon Brief that the fund’s board deals with most funding requests as regular projects, rather than emergencies. Singh continues:

“Developed countries gave a really cold response to Nepal’s request. They have not addressed it because they know that if this happens once, they are going to be under pressure all the time. This is unacceptable.”

Meanwhile, BBC News reported that Nepal plans to use climate attribution studies to strengthen its claim.

According to a rapid attribution study by World Weather Attribution and climate experts who spoke to Carbon Brief, factors such as glacial retreat and permafrost thaw that played a key role in the disaster have been linked to climate change. A full attribution study is pending.

Nepal’s prime minister Balendra Shah will address the UN general assembly on 24 September and is expected to raise issues around climate justice, loss and damage and the vulnerability of mountain countries.



The next board meeting of the loss and damage fund is on 15 December, two months from now, and a fortnight after the conclusion of COP31 in Turkey.

Pandit Chhetri tells Carbon Brief:

“It’s a shame that, until now, the fund has not been able to even give a penny to developing countries. And, starkly, the event in Nepal only demonstrates why this kind of fund is so important for highly vulnerable, poor, developing countries.”

Pandit Chhetri adds that, after nearly three weeks since the disaster, there is yet to be a decision on the request and that the country has “only received messages of solidarity”, with no assurance of rapid response funds. He says that it is “quite an interesting scene for [us] to observe”, adding:

“If the fund cannot respond in a crisis like this for a country like Nepal – when you have this massive destruction and devastation – then what is the use of the fund itself? That’s why it is a test for the fund, though the resources are limited.”

description: 275 Indians Still Missing After Nepal Floods as Forensic Teams Work to Identify Victims  INDIA New England News
publisher.title: INDIA New England News
full_article:
New Delhi — As many as 275 Indian nationals remain missing following devastating flash floods in Nepal, while forensic teams continue efforts to identify victims, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said Tuesday.

MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said an Indian forensic team is working alongside Nepali experts in Kathmandu laboratories and has been examining thousands of samples.

“As I told you last time, we had given you a figure of 275 people who are missing Indian nationals or over and above, there were several other people from the Indian diaspora, persons of Indian origin, who are also missing. We have a forensic team in Nepal which is working in Kathmandu in several laboratories along with their Nepali colleagues. They have been working on 3,000 samples, of which they have been able to arrive at 1,200 DNA profiles, so the work is going on and on the missing Indian nationals we await to hear from Nepali authorities,” Jaiswal said during the ministry’s weekly media briefing.

India has also provided relief supplies and rescue personnel to Nepal following requests from the government in Kathmandu.

“So, on this, I would like to say that, as you know, when this incident happened, since then, we have provided assistance from our side based on the requests received from them. This included relief material, as well as the rescue teams that we sent there, about which you already know. We sent a team of 54 people there. Some people are still working there, while some have returned. The Government of Nepal is currently assessing the situation there,” Jaiswal said.

The 54-member Indian team included 30 tunnel rescue experts, 19 forensic specialists and a five-member medical team.

An Indian Air Force flight carrying 11 tons of supplies arrived in Kathmandu on Saturday and was handed over to the Nepalese government. It was the ninth special flight India has dispatched with relief materials, equipment and expert personnel since the floods struck on Aug. 26. (Source: IANS)

title: As loss and damage fund stalls, Nepal crowdfunds flood relief - Climate Home News
description: As loss and damage fund stalls, Nepal crowdfunds flood relief  Climate Home News
publisher.title: Climate Home News
full_article:
People around the world have donated almost $90 million to a government-led campaign to help Nepal recover from its recent devastating Himalayan flood, according to a Nepali climate negotiator, even as the UN chief slammed the tiny amount of money in a new fund to deal with such disasters.

Individuals and companies from Nepal and abroad have chipped in from $5 to "many millions" of dollars to the Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund, Manjeet Dhakal, an advisor to the poorest countries at UN climate talks, told an event on Monday focused on early warning systems.

The prompt and substantial response from the public contrasts with the slower, more limited support that is potentially on offer from the UN's new Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), set up by governments to compensate developing countries for climate disasters.

Comment: Human security relies on adapting to the world’s new climate reality

Over three weeks have passed since Nepal's finance and environment ministers asked the FRLD board to take an urgent decision to allocate funding to help Nepal protect people and restore essential services in the wake of the disaster, which caused around 1,450 deaths and left more than 5,000 people missing.

"Time is of the essence," the ministers wrote in an appeal to the FRLD on August 31, which was swiftly followed by a letter from a group of developing-country board members urging the FRLD board's co-chairs to organise an extraordinary meeting to come up with a response.

Loss and damage fund hesitates

Yet, despite informal online meetings, the co-chairs have yet to convene a meeting with the power to allocate funds. The board's next scheduled meeting begins on December 15.

Dhakal said on Monday that the request has "received some positive response, but still there is some discussion ongoing about how to respond to that".

"If they can't respond in a timely manner, then is [the fund] fit for purpose in terms of disasters that the world would be facing in the coming years? The scale and intensity of these disasters is increasing," he said.

With just $820 million pledged to it by rich countries and not all of that yet delivered, the FRLD has earmarked just $350 million to spend in its initial phase and without further contributions could run out of money next year.

Because of these limited funds, and a huge number of requests for funding totalling nearly $3 billion, the FRLD has said it will only give out a maximum of $20 million to each project for now. It has yet to approve funding for any projects.

Dhakal recently told The Nation magazine that this amount was just a "symbolic gesture". Nepal's government has estimated the costs of recovery and reconstruction at $4.8 billion, with homes, roads, bridges, hospitals and hydropower stations in the affected area needing to be repaired and rebuilt.

"Ridiculously small" funding

In a speech to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, the body's outgoing Secretary-General António Guterres criticised the "ridiculously small" level of funds made available by wealthy governments to the FRLD. Developed countries should "make the loss and damage fund work at scale", he said.

Secretary-General António Guterres speaks at UNGA (Photo: UN Photo/ Loey Felipe)

The Portuguese diplomat told world leaders that when he travelled to Nepal three years ago, he had "sounded the alarm on accelerating glacier melt, warning that the rooftops of the world are caving in".

"Some dismissed it all as overstating dangers, but as tragic events have shown, impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder, and spreading further than many anticipated," he said.

A recent study by scientists with the World Weather Attribution group found that climate change contributed to the rock-ice avalanche which sparked a huge flash flood along a river valley on the Nepal-Tibet border.

Speaking at a separate event in New York on Monday, leading climate scientist Johan Rockström highlighted those findings on the role of global warming in the Himalayan disaster.

"This will be potentially the first poster-child case of a loss and damage invoice, because here we have a proven case of a catastrophe which would not have occurred if it hadn't been for human-caused climate change," he said.

title: Foreign Ministers of Nepal and Maldives Hold Bilateral Talks in New York - Ratopati
description: Foreign Ministers of Nepal and Maldives Hold Bilateral Talks in New York  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal and Maldives Foreign Minister Iruthisham Adams held bilateral talks.

During the meeting held in New York on the occasion of the 81st General Assembly of the United Nations, Minister Khanal expressed his heartfelt gratitude to the Maldivian government and people for the sympathy, solidarity, and humanitarian assistance provided following the recent devastating floods in Nepal.

During the meeting, the two Foreign Ministers exchanged views on Nepal-Maldives bilateral relations, regional and multilateral issues.

They discussed ways to further strengthen bilateral relations between the two countries by exchanging high-level visits and expanding cooperation in areas such as tourism, employment, and education, according to the secretariat of Foreign Minister Khanal.

Similarly, both ministers emphasized the need to make cooperation between Nepal and Maldives more effective on issues of mutual interest and concern, including climate change, mobilizing financial resources for development, and sustainable development.

Discussions were also held on continuing cooperation and coordination on issues of common interest in multilateral forums such as the United Nations and the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).

title: The Patagonia town where Nepal’s deadly glacier flood could be repeated – and what they’ve learned - theguardian.com
description: The Patagonia town where Nepal’s deadly glacier flood could be repeated – and what they’ve learned  theguardian.com
publisher.title: theguardian.com
full_article:
T he images from Nepal stopped Daniela Schmidt in her tracks. A geologist at the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina, she watched the deadly flash floods on 26 August tear through everything in their path, people running for their lives as the water and debris swept over the landscape.

“I had never seen anything like it,” she says. “This was one of the most catastrophic events on a global scale related to these glacial floods.”

View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the Nepal floods in Nuwakot district, 26 August. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

The shock deepened as the first geological figures emerged: the volume of glacier ice and rock that had collapsed and the scale of the resulting flow. Schmidt began comparing them with the cases she had studied during her PhD. Very few glacial lake outburst floods, she realised, had reached anything close to this magnitude.

But Nepal also changed the way she saw her own work. Schmidt studies the glacial lake outburst flood (Glof) that could occur at Laguna Torre, in Argentina’s Santa Cruz province, and its potential impact on El Chaltén, a nearby town known as the country’s trekking capital.

The disaster already exists on her computer screen: data, models, flood simulations and maps. According to her studies, if the northern slope of Cerro Solo were to collapse into Laguna Torre, at the base of the Torre glacier, a massive volume of water could travel the 5 miles (8km) to El Chaltén in 20 minutes, sweeping along logs, rocks and sediment.

Map of the Torre glacier and Torre glacier

The discharge could reach 1,769 cubic metres (62,472 cubic feet) a second, rushing down the Fitz Roy River towards the town and inundating its only access bridge and other critical infrastructure. For anyone in the valley, those 20 minutes would be the window to reach safety. “It is the worst-case flood scenario,” says Schmidt, adding that, in the most conservative analysis, the flow would take between 45 minutes and an hour to reach the town.

“You can’t say it will happen on a specific day or at a specific time, but society needs to be prepared,” Schmidt warns. “It is going to happen.”

View image in fullscreen Sustained melting has created a second body of water within Laguna Torre, which poses a risk to the town below if the glacier collapses. Photograph: Javier Rasetti

The threat was already changing how El Chaltén prepared for the future, but the disaster in Nepal has brought these risks to the forefront. Although the scale of that event and the El Chaltén scenario differ, Schmidt sees a similarity in the mechanism: a mass suddenly plunging into a body of water can trigger a flash flood with immense destructive power.

Authorities from Los Glaciares national park and the municipality of El Chaltén, along with local organisations and various scientific institutions, are working to develop the country’s first Glof early-warning system and draft evacuation protocols.

“We are preparing for the worst-case scenario,” says Enrique Rivero, El Chaltén’s secretary of government.

T he silhouette of Cerro Solo is unmistakable. The vertical granite peak, rising to 2,121 metres (6,959ft) above sea level, is reflected in Laguna Torre amid floating icebergs. That is where the risk begins.

View image in fullscreen As the ice on the Torre glacier retreats, the surrounding slopes can also shift. Photograph: Javier Rasetti

The Torre glacier is estimated to have lost 4 sq km (1.5 sq miles) of surface area, while its ice thinned by 60-70 metres between 1952 and 2023. As the ice retreats, the balance of the surrounding slopes also shifts – a process researchers describe as a “release of stress”.

This transformation is visible in landslides and rockfalls that leave scars across the mountainside. Between 2002 and 2023, the volume of displaced material increased, while the speed of movement doubled. “It moves slowly, but during heavy rainfall or high temperatures, it accelerates in pulses,” Schmidt says. “As the slopes become unstable, they can slide, dumping a large volume of material into the lake and causing it to overflow. It just needs a trigger.”

Her models contemplate landslides involving between 8m and 13m cubic metres of material. If a mass of that size were to collapse into Laguna Torre, it could generate a wave up to 5.8 metres high. The wave would travel across the lake at approximately 20 metres a second, reaching the Fitz Roy River in just one minute and 40 seconds.

Under the most conservative and the worst-case scenarios, a flood would eventually reach the bridge and render it unusable. The bridge is the only land access connecting El Chaltén to provincial route 41.

The municipality has already ordered the dredging of the river channel and the clearing of the riverbed beneath the bridge. “But now we are being told that the water level could rise by up to 5 metres, which suggests the bridge could be swept away,” Rivero says.

View image in fullscreen Fitz Roy River in the Laguna Torre valley. The river could rise rapidly by up to 5 metres if a glacial lake outburst flood occurred. Photograph: Javier Rasetti

The flood could also affect critical infrastructure located just metres from the riverbanks, including gas and power plants, schools and homes. Discussions have already begun on a contingency plan that considers, among other measures, potential relocation.

“Gas supplies coming from Río Gallegos – the capital of Santa Cruz province – would be cut off, leaving us without heating,” says Paula Chaparro, a member of the El Chaltén Mountain Guides Association. “If the power grid fails, El Chaltén relies on generators running on fuel oil; if they run out of fuel, we lose electricity. It’s a problematic chain reaction.”

If the event were to occur in summer, peaking in December to February, the town would be cut off, with more than 27,000 people – locals and tourists alike – stranded in the town. At present, according to residents, there is no signage indicating evacuation routes or instructions, nor do hotels warn guests about the risk.

The risk has been known for years, but the available instruments could not precisely determine how quickly the slope was moving or, crucially, how much water could be displaced in a collapse. “We’ll have to wait and see if it happens” was a common reaction among locals, says Sofía Bonangelino, a member of Friends of Los Glaciares National Park, an association that manages three campsites.

View image in fullscreen The Fitz Roy River bridge, which provides the only access to the town of El Chaltén. Photograph: Javier Rasetti

Even Horacio Pelozo, the park superintendent, acknowledges this: “The initial studies really weren’t alarming, or anything of the sort.”

However, a key new piece of data emerged, Pelozo says, alongside the measurements of the slope’s movement: sustained melting had created a second body of water within Laguna Torre, the depth of which now exceeds 220 metres. Previous estimates had placed the depth at about 80 metres.

View image in fullscreen The remains of Blatten in Switzerland after the collapse of the Birch glacier, 29 May 2025. Photograph: Jean-Christophe Bott/AP

Then, in May 2025, an image from the Swiss Alps demonstrated the potential scale of a collapse involving ice and rock: the Birch glacier collapsed on to much of the village of Blatten, burying it in a matter of seconds.

Los Glaciares national park has taken steps to address the risk of a Glof, including relocating the De Agostini campsite, rerouting hiking trails, installing warning signs and establishing an evacuation protocol involving at least 25 personnel to manage potential floods during peak visitor seasons.

The response has expanded to include coordination with local and national agencies, such as the municipality of El Chaltén, in the Santa Cruz province, the Federal Emergency Agency and the Argentine Geological and Mining Service, though no formal contingency plan has been finalised yet.

The El Chaltén city council has passed a resolution to develop an evacuation plan, while a detection system with six monitoring stations – equipped with cameras, sensors and emergency buoys – is in development to trigger alerts via sirens, SMS and email. Yet funding cuts have delayed implementation, with the estimated cost of $220,000 (£163,000) exceeding the park’s current capacity, as noted by Eduardo Marino, a former secretary of government for El Chaltén.

“Let’s not talk about Glofs, because it will scare off tourists” – that concern is circulating around town. And it is not hard to understand why – a large part of the community relies on tourism for its livelihood.

View image in fullscreen El Chaltén seen from the beginning of the Laguna Torre trail, which is popular with hikers. Photograph: Javier Rasetti

Marino owns a hotel; Bonangelino runs a bookstore, rents out a cabin, and works as a ski instructor. For them, as for so many other residents, protecting tourism also means protecting their own livelihoods.

View image in fullscreen Eduardo Marino who owns a hotel in El Chaltén. Photograph: Javier Rasetti

Marino was asked to drop the subject until the summer season was over. He refused. He knows a day of heavy rain or exceptionally high temperatures could be enough to trigger an event they are not yet prepared for.

For those who work in the mountains, information is key to risk management. “Closing down isn’t the solution,” says Chaparro. The idea, she says, is to offer alternatives: different trails, different activities. “It’s not about being afraid; it’s about staying alert.”

High risk yet home to thousands: the makeshift towns at the mercy of landslides and floods in Peru Read more

When her colleague Ariel Puntin speaks to local people about the threat he still encounters some who doubt the mountainside could collapse. The problem, he says, is that the gap between “it could happen today” and “it might never happen” is too wide to easily learn how to live with the risk.

View image in fullscreen The Fitz Roy River flooding could affect gas and power plants built near its banks, as well as homes and businesses. Photograph: Javier Rasetti

For Schmidt, the events in Nepal should serve as a wake-up call, but also as an opportunity to improve the town’s preparedness. “The community and the tourists must be protected and kept safe in the face of this new reality of constantly changing glacial landscapes,” she says.

Bonangelino has noticed a positive shift in recent months. As the studies’ findings have been explained to the community, she says, acceptance has grown that the phenomenon is real and that preparation is necessary.

“We are a resilient, responsible community that cares deeply about its environment,” she says. “We rely on tourism, and we aren’t going to neglect it.”
